bugs.summary: Improve logical subscript performance: x[x > 0.5] runs 1.8 to 2.9 times as fast

comments.creator: kevinushey
comments.text:
## Summary

`x[x > 0.5]` on a million doubles runs 1.8 to 2.9 times as fast with this patch, and logical subscripts are 32% to 43% faster in the geometric mean over 40 cases, measured on macOS, Linux (aarch64 and x86_64) and Windows. Enhancement: a performance change, results do not change.

## Details

`logicalSubscript()` in `src/main/subscript.c` fills a temporary buffer in a loop that branches on every element of the subscript, then allocates the index vector and copies the buffer. When the subscript comes from a comparison on unsorted data, that branch is mispredicted for about every second element.

Benchmark: attached as `logical-subscript-bench.R`; on macOS it prints 3.5 ms per call of `x[x > 0.5]` before the patch and 1.3 ms after, and 2.7 ms against 0.53 ms for a random half-`TRUE` mask.

Proposed patch: attached as `logical-subscript-fill.diff`; it counts the selected elements, allocates the index at its exact length, skips blocks that are all `FALSE` and stores the rest without a branch on the data. It adds a regression test; `make check-devel` passes at r90960, and the patch applies unchanged to r90971.

The patch is also submitted as https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/pull/526, which has the benchmark tables for all four systems, including the cases that gain little.

## AI Disclosure

This patch was prepared with the assistance of Claude Code. I used Claude to explore optimizations of this code using branchless programming and vectorization opportunities the compiler was missing.

comments.text:
A note on one part of the patch that may look unusual. `isAllFalse()` tests a block of eight elements as four 64-bit words, read through `memcpy()`:

```
uint64_t w;
memcpy(&w, ps + j, sizeof w);
any |= w;
```

Words are used so that the test does not depend on the vectorizer: gcc on aarch64 does not vectorize the plain loop `any |= ps[j]`. `memcpy()` is used because reading `int` objects through a `uint64_t *` breaks C's aliasing rules, and the words are not always 8-byte aligned. It costs nothing: gcc 13.3 (x86_64 and aarch64) and Apple clang emit no call to `memcpy` at `-O0` to `-O2`, and at `-O2` generate code equivalent to a cast's.

References:

- John Regehr, "Type Punning, Strict Aliasing, and Optimization": https://blog.regehr.org/archives/959
- John Regehr, "The Strict Aliasing Situation is Pretty Bad": https://blog.regehr.org/archives/1307
- GCC manual, `-fstrict-aliasing`: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Optimize-Options.html#index-fstrict-aliasing
- Linux kernel documentation, "Unaligned Memory Accesses": https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/unaligned-memory-access.html

comments.text:
Created attachment 4160
patch v2: count first and fill the index without a data-dependent branch (against r90971)

I've refreshed the patch after a review pass over the PR; it replaces attachment 4158. The fill now returns at once when nothing is selected (all-`FALSE` subscripts are 30 to 49% faster than with the first patch), the counting loop checks for interrupts, and the regression test also covers recycled and over-long subscripts and matrix rows.

One design point: the index is sized in one pass over the subscript and filled in a second, so the subscript must not change in between. In theory it could, for example an ALTREP vector over shared memory that another process writes to; the fill could then overrun the index, where the old non-recycled loop read each element once. I think such use is already unsupported (the recycled path, and `x[i] <- v` with an integer `i`, make the same assumption), and it may be worth documenting that for ALTREP classes.

`make check` passes on macOS. The patch is against r90971 and matches https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/pull/526.
